attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The revision restores his 'can't be a recipe for success' wording. Classing it as an undated causal objection to building robots on low-comprehension language models is a fair reading.

contract.note: Reading success as dependable, safe household performance fits the post's context. The contract rightly says he gave no measure of comprehension and no success threshold, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: 2022 Inner Monologue study: environment feedback improved LLM planning. It does not show dependable household operation, and it does not isolate world comprehension as the cause either way.

May 2026 benchmark that sets aside physical control and uses a different, memory-augmented system. Low full-task success is consistent with his view but does not test the 2022 architecture's causal limit.

reviews.rationale: Neither item isolates limited world comprehension as what prevents dependable robot performance. Neither shows LLM-based robots performing safely and dependably across varied households. The packet does not meet the support or contradiction condition, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: His own sentence. The Craddock tweets are quoted context, but this concluding judgment is Marcus's.

semantics.note: It keeps the 'no reason to think exempt' framing and the scope of robots with language interfaces. 'These problems' correctly covers both open-ended edge cases and forgetting.

contract.note: Reading this as a claim of susceptibility, not of inevitable forgetting, is an ordinary and fair reading. The contract sets the 2022 research window through the post date as an inference of its own, and says so.

evidence.note: The August 2022 SayCan paper reports a failure on negated instructions that the system inherited from its language model. That shows the language-interface robot is not exempt from failures outside what it handles reliably.
The March 2022 AirLoop paper treats catastrophic forgetting as a real problem for learned robot components trained sequentially. Its mitigation reduces the problem but does not show exemption.

reviews.rationale: Research from within the window shows the Google-style system failing on instructions it did not handle reliably, and robotics work treating forgetting in learned components as a live issue. Nothing in the packet shows that robots or language interfaces remove these vulnerabilities. The support condition is met, but on susceptibility only: there is no direct test of forgetting in PaLM-SayCan.

attribution.note: His own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the core claim about underestimated difficulty. Dropping the background clause about decades of demos does not change what he commits to.

contract.note: Reading 'most people' as prominent public and industry expectations is the ordinary reading and is not stretched for or against him. The period ends at the post date, which is appropriate.

evidence.note: A 2019 WIRED report: Ford's CEO said the industry overestimated the arrival of self-driving cars because the problem is complex. It also covers retreating forecasts at several companies.
Brin's 2012 optimistic but qualified forecast. It is background on expectations, not an outcome.
Waymo's own 2020 announcement of fully driverless public rides in Phoenix. This restricted-area service qualifies the post's 'only experimental' remark but does not refute underestimated difficulty.
A 2015 CMU retrospective on the 1995 demo. It confirms the decades of demonstrations and notes some researchers expected gradual progress.

reviews.rationale: Before the post, prominent expectations were publicly revised: Ford, Nissan's 2020 promise and Waymo's CEO all pulled back, citing complexity, across more than one optimistic forecast. Actual deployment by 2022 was geofenced and limited, well short of claims like thousands of fully autonomous Ford vehicles by 2021. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: He restates his own 2016 view and says he still thinks it is true, so he endorses it in 2022.

semantics.note: 'Won't be enough' is firm, so this is a scored forecast with no deadline. The sentence just before it is hedged ('not all that likely'), but the claimed sentence itself is unqualified. Reading 'enough' as 'more data alone' is fair.

contract.note: Reading the claim in its household-robot context, with sufficiency of data as the test, is fair. 'Solve', 'big data' and 'data-only' are undefined, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: A 2024 study: diversity of training data improves generalization on bounded single tasks. It does not show that data alone solves household robotics.
Physical Intelligence's own April 2026 claim of better generalization. It is not independent, does not isolate data scaling, and does not show broadly reliable household competence.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was given, and no dated event meets the early-resolution rule. Neither item shows data scaling alone delivering reliable household robots, and neither shows rigorously that it cannot. Continued failures and elapsed time do not count as decisive, so the forecast is unresolved.
